scenes.heading: Backfills & Reprocessing
scenes.narration: A backfill reprocesses historical data to fix or fill it, and doing it safely at scale is a core reliability skill.

scenes.heading: When you need a backfill
bullets: A bug corrupted a range of past partitions
A new column or table needs historical values
Business logic changed and history must reflect it
scenes.narration: You backfill when a bug corrupted a range of past partitions and needs correcting. You also backfill to populate a newly added column or table with historical values. Late-arriving events force reprocessing of already-closed windows, and a change in business logic sometimes means history itself must be recomputed.

scenes.heading: A safe backfill process
scenes.narration: Start by scoping the exact date range so you do not touch more data than necessary. Run the backfill into a staging copy rather than overwriting production directly. Validate the staged result against production before you swap or merge it in atomically, and throttle the job so it never starves your live pipelines of resources.

scenes.heading: In-place vs staged backfill
scenes.narration: An in-place backfill overwrites the live tables directly, which is fast but leaves you with no easy way to recover if it goes wrong. A staged backfill writes to a separate copy first, lets you validate the numbers, and only then swaps it in. The staged approach trades a little speed for a clean rollback path.

scenes.text: Backfills rely on idempotency: partition your work, validate before swapping in, and throttle so you never take down live pipelines.
scenes.narration: Safe backfills lean on idempotency, so partition your work, validate before swapping the results in, and throttle carefully so a backfill never takes down your live pipelines.
